Subject: Performance / SLO qualification — latency & throughput targets (recap + next steps)

Alex / Priya — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can size Dedicated capacity and validate cost targets.

TL;DR / ask:
- Target: p95 latency <= 250ms for 512-token requests (streaming enabled)
- Expected qps: 60 sustained, spike to 200 for 30s during peak events
- Concurrency target per customer session: up to 8 simultaneous streams
- Primary concerns: streaming tail latency, and cost per 1k tokens

What we covered:
- Your main flows are interactive chat with streaming + some batch embedding jobs for search indexing.
- You prefer to keep model weights on dedicated pool (no shared instances).
- Success metric: <250ms p95 for generation start; end-to-end streaming experience should not feel laggy.

Initial Redwood thoughts (high-level levers to hit SLO while controlling cost):
1) Continuous batching: use fine-grained batching for short-window workloads to increase GPU utilization without adding significant queuing latency.
2) KV / prefix caching: cache common system prompts and shared prefixes across similar sessions to avoid re-computing initial tokens.
3) Quantization profiles: run evaluation of 4-bit quantized variant for 90% of inference, fall back to FP16 for high-quality or long-context cases.
4) Model variants & routing: route low-latency interactive traffic to a smaller trimmed model variant (faster kernels) and reserve full-model for heavy completion/backfill jobs.
5) Streaming optimizations: tune generation chunk size + kernel selection to reduce first-chunk latency.
6) Autoscale + burst pools: keep a small dedicated hot pool sized for baseline and allow short burst capacity for spikes.

Next steps I propose:
- Rishi to run a quick profiling session on your sample payloads (can you share ~100 representative requests + average token lengths?) — we have an example-payload.json attached.
- You to confirm the p95 latency vs throughput tradeoff you care about (is 250ms p95 strict, or is 300ms acceptable during 90s of peak?).
- We'll produce an initial cost estimate with batching/caching knobs and a recommended Dedicated pool configuration.

Attachments: SLO_requirements.xlsx (your answers), example-payload.json (sample payloads), network-diagram.png

Thanks — Marissa

Subject: Re: Performance / SLO qualification — latency & throughput targets (technical notes)

Alex — quick technical notes based on the payload and targets. Short answers first: continuous batching can be configured to keep queue latency under 10-20ms for short prompts with proper max-batch window; quantized 4-bit models typically add negligible hallucination regression for classification/completion tasks we saw in similar domains, but we should validate on your eval set.

Detailed notes:
- Latency math: p95 = service_queue + model_first_chunk + decode_chunk_time + network. For 512-token-ish completions, first-chunk generation dominates in our profiling. We can hit ~180–220ms p95 on A100-class GPUs for optimized kernels with small batch sizes and stream chunk=8 tokens.
- Continuous batching: set max-latency window = 8ms and max-batch-size proportional to observed qps. That keeps per-request added queuing to single-digit ms at moderate load. Under spike-to-200 qps, short bursts may push queue addl ~20–40ms if we want to keep utilization high; autoscale + burst pool reduces that.
- Caching: prefix/KV caching for repeated system prompts and commonly-shared prefixes can reduce compute by ~25–40% for your flows. We can whitelist prompts to ensure cache hits for the interactive app.
- Quantization profiles: we recommend evaluating Q4-LO and Q4-HY profiles. Typical tradeoff: 20–30% cost reduction vs FP16 with <2% drop in relevant evaluation metrics for many workloads; your domain-specific prompts need validation.
- Model variants/routing: route low-latency interactive traffic to a trimmed decoder-only variant or a lower-dimension profile for cheap fast generation; fallback to full model for heavy completion. This can shave ~30% of latency at comparable quality for short outputs.

Actionables from my side:
- I'll run a short microbenchmark against the example-payload.json tomorrow and share a profiling report (includes first-chunk times, bytes per chunk, and recommended chunk size).
- I'll also produce two config options: (A) low-latency hot pool + burst autoscale (recommended for interactive launch); (B) cost-optimized steady pool with aggressive batching (recommended for non-peak windows).

If you can confirm that 350ms is an acceptable guardrail during launches, I'll size the burst capacity accordingly.

-rishi
